question: At autopsy, shotgun pellets recovered from a victim show a tight cluster with a spread of approximately 4 cm. The shotgun barrel has a full choke. Which forensic inference is most appropriate?

answers.text: The muzzle was pressed against the skin at time of discharge.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A contact discharge would show a stellate laceration, extensive blackening, gas inflation of the wound, and typically no pellet spread pattern — full choke constriction is irrelevant at contact range.

answers.text: The shot was fired from a close range of approximately 1–2 metres.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Full choke concentrates pellets over a longer distance. A 4 cm spread at full choke is consistent with a range of approximately 1–2 metres. The tighter the choke, the smaller the spread at any given distance, which directly informs range estimation.

answers.text: The shot was fired from a range exceeding 10 metres.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: At distances beyond 10 metres, even full choke would produce a spread well exceeding 4 cm. The tight cluster indicates a shorter range.

answers.text: The choke degree has no bearing on range estimation.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Choke degree is a critical variable in range estimation for shotgun wounds. Full choke produces the tightest spread; cylinder bore produces the widest. Ignoring choke would render pellet-spread-based range estimation unreliable.

overallFeedback.feedback: Reconsider: choke narrows the pellet spread. A full-choke tight cluster at 4 cm diameter indicates short-range (1–2 m) firing rather than contact or distant fire.

Well analysed. Choke constriction directly modifies pellet dispersion at any given range — full choke at close range gives a deceptively tight pattern that mimics distant but unChooked fire. Always note the choke degree in your medicolegal report.
